utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I trust that the Court has been informed briefly that there was a problem -- is a problem with the witness schedule for today. Mr. Samardzic, as obvious to those of us dealing with him yesterday, that although he was resolute about his willingness to give evidence as soon as possibly required, he was suffering some ill health, and on his return to his hotel it became absolutely clear that he was indeed unwell. Various domestic arrangements have to be made for him. I expect he will be fit -- well, it's in the nature of the man to say that he's fit -- as soon as possible. I expect that he actually will be fit comparatively soon - one would hope tomorrow - but nothing can be certain, and we'll have more information later this morning or probably later today. Once it became obvious to us that he shouldn't try to give evidence today, we made arrangements to see whether Mr. Matovina could be available, and he could. I was unable to contact the accused by any means other than ultimately direct contact through the head of the Detention Unit, and I understand that he will have told the accused at probably sometime after 7.00 last night that this change was a possibility. Accordingly, we would ask that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff takes Mr. Matovina next. As to Samardzic, as the Chamber knows, I'm not going to be back until probably quarter to ten or 10.00 tomorrow morning. I would prefer, if he's fit tomorrow morning, and we shan't know that of course until this afternoon, to take him if the Chamber's prepared to accommodate us. Apart from him, there are two other witnesses available for some time this week although neither of them is going to be available first thing tomorrow morning because they will not have arrived until just about then. I'm not sure whether Mr. Matovina will take all of today's hearing time or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina deals with Slatina. Again, a map would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just intervene on the topic of the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far we have provided someone, and I can't remember where it is now, with a road atlas. I don't know if it found its way to the Bench. It's got a lot of other material in it other than a road atlas and was rather heavier and thicker than the similar document in Kosovo. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It had been shown to me. I don't know whether anybody else has seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if that's the sort of document, in the absence of anything more focused, that would be helpful. If it is, we will -- we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll go and get some more so the Chamber can have one each, along with everybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be available, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think so. I think that or something similar. There must be road atlases. Frankly, I'd prefer to try to find a road atlas that covered both Croatia and Bosnia in the same volume because I think that would be pretty helpful, and the combined geographical area is not so large as to make that improbable. It's an index which is, of course, most useful for the Chamber, I suspect, amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have this, if it is available, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll check on its availability. And if it or something broadly similar to it is, I'll acquire enough copies for everybody to have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how long do you approximate Mr. Matovina will be in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two hours in chief is Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's calculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He produces quite a lot of exhibits, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I notice for some reason that mine begins -- seems to begin at tab -- I may be wrong about that. Tab 1. Yes, I see. Yes. And the accused would not have found out about the change until last evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So he really won't have had any time to prepare his cross-examination, or very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On the other hand, the hope is that Mr. Samardzic should be ready tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the hope, and we'll wait -- simply have to wait and see. We've prevailed on him to see a doctor. He's, again, the sort of person who, despite all his problems, is minded just to press on, but we've prevailed on him to see a doctor today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you would have available the next two witnesses - I'm looking at the list - K-1 and Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But not first thing tomorrow morning. Later on; Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When was the accused given the statement of Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A long time ago. Oh, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Last Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It had been disclosed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It had been disclosed before but it was redisclosed because he was maintaining he couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So as far as the order is concerned, the statement was disclosed some time ago and you're in compliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But the more immediate problem, of course, is his preparation. Well, there seems to be no objection to hearing Mr. Matovina at least in chief or in direct. He seems now to be called. We'll hear Mr. Milosevic about cross-examination. Mr. Milosevic, you've heard the position that the first witness is ill. He clearly can't be ready today. Are you in a position to cross-examine Mr. Matovina this morning or are you going to ask for more time? It may be simplest, in fact, to hear Mr. Matovina and then to consider the position as to whether you need more time to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what do you say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no requests or demands, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes. Let's call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please state your name, age, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: My name is Dzuro Matovina. I was born on the 22nd of March, 1949, in Slatina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I am a criminal investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you work as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Thirty years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work during the years 1990 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: In Podravska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is it situated? Is that in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Podravska Slatina is located on the main road from Virovitica to Osijek. It's 100 kilometres away from Osijek and 30 from Virovitica. It is in the Bishopric of Podravska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We do not need so detailed information. I just wanted to know, it is in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, in the area of Western Slavonia, bordering on Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your rank in the years 1990 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I was a police inspector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in fact the acting chief of police in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, until 1989. Until just before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the events, did you continue to be in the police? I mean the war.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. I remained on the police force, and I was assistant chief of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get involved in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. My job was in Slatina, and I coordinated the work of the police in law enforcement in the area of Slatina and further afield. I did not take any part in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of Podravska Slatina in 1990, before the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: On the territory of the former municipality of Podravska Slatina, there were 56 or, rather, 57 percent of Croats, 36 per cent of Serbs, and the rest was a mixture of other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the relationship between the ethnic groups good before the war?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Relations among ethnic groups before the war were tolerable. However, after the first multi-party elections were held following 45 years of communist rule, when the first multi-party Croat parliament was elected, inter-ethnic relations became very complicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a branch of the SDS party founded at some point in time in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: That is correct. A branch of the Serbian Democratic Party was founded in Slatina on the 9th of June, 1990. However, just before the party was established, there was a series of provocations in Slatina leading to ethnic tensions, and the leadership and the founding committee of the SDS carried out propaganda and psychological activities which contributed to these ethnic tensions. That happened on the 31st of May, the night between the 31st of May and the 1st of June, 1990, when in Batici, Donji Melani, Spanat, Medinci, Sladojevci and a number of other neighbouring villages, the facades of many buildings were marked by graffiti which were actually slogans expressing ethnic slurs and hatred. Some of this graffiti said, "We will kill Tudjman," and others said, "Serbia is from here to Karlobag," or "Serbia all the way to the Una River." There were also drawings of four Cyrillic "S" symbols. Vuk Draskovic's name written on buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you here. We would not need so many details. Therefore, I would ask you to just answer my questions briefly. Was there a founding rally in -- of the SDS in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. The rally was held on the 9th of June, 1990, in a clearing, from 4.00 to 7.00 p.m., and it was attended by about 5.000 Serbs from Slatina and the neighbouring settlements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this rally were there also people from outside of Western Slavonia or Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a number of people from the neighbouring villages, and there were also people with strange appearance who were not familiar to us in Slatina. There were Jovan Raskovic, Mr. Opacic, and other speakers invited to the rally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jovan Raskovic and Jovan Opacic, who were they? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They were leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party. They had come at the invitation of the founding committee of the SDS for Slatina, and they were the main speakers at that rally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to Mr. Raskovic, you said he was the main -- one of the main speakers. During his speech, did he speak about the situation of the Serbs in Croatia? And if so, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Jovan Raskovic's speech was another speech of hatred, inciting hatred between the Serbs and Croats living in that area. Among other things he said, I remember one. He said that there is no future for Serbs in the Independent State of Croatia, that another Ustasha government is in power, that if Serbs want autonomy and ask for it, they should have it. And he ended his speech with the words, "Serb brothers, see you in Krajina. You will have no happiness in the Ustasha state."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean, "See you in Krajina"? What did he refer to?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, according to what followed later, this was supposed to mean in an area that would secede from the Republic of Croatia and that would later be annexed - the way it turned out, according to the referenda that were held - that would be annexed to Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he address that already in the speech?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: His speech and the speeches of the members of the initiative committee showed it quite clearly what this was all about and what the intention was of that particular rally and all other activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the speakers mention whether the Serbs and the Croats would live together in the future? Was that addressed at all?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: It was mentioned that Serbs could no longer live together with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Croats in an Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the speech, did he -- did Mr. Raskovic or other people, did they refer to the position of Slatina, what Slatina would be in the future?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: President of SDS of Slatina, Milun Karadzic, who was elected there, he also spoke at this rally. After the rally, members of the SDS were spreading a feeling of fear among the population that Slatina should actually become the Slavonian Knin, the centre of the rebellion in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Karadzic, Milun Karadzic. Who else was a leading figure in the SDS, the local SDS in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, there was Ilija Sasic, then Simpraga Vladimir, Rajko Bojcic, Jovan Bojcic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. That should be enough. The speakers, did they make any references to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was not mentioned, as far as I can remember. However, what was dominant was the paraphernalia, including pictures of Mr. Milosevic and several persons unknown. Actually, several unknown persons were wearing the flags of the Republic of Serbia like scarves, and others were wearing cockades on their caps, and that was reminiscent of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time period following this founding rally, were referenda organised?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. Three referenda were organised in the second half of 1990. All three were organised whenever the Croatian parliament organised referenda with regard to the status of the Republic of Croatia within the former Yugoslavia. That is to say that these referenda were held before the other referenda, which additionally complicated things for the public or, rather, inter-ethnic relations. The first referendum was held on the 26th of August --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. We do not go into the details of the -- of this because it was already addressed with another witness, but can you tell me, could the Croat population participate in these referenda that were held by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. Croats did not take part in these referenda because they were illegal. Because the first referendum was held in the following way: Activists of the SDS went to various houses, and the others were held in public places, that is to say in offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it -- what -- I would like to know, were the Croats not interested in voting or were they not allowed to vote?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They were not even invited to vote in the referendum. As I've already said, the referenda were illegal. Croats and other Serbs who accepted the government in the Republic of Croatia went to the referenda that were organised by the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the police or any Croatian institution try to prevent or interfere with the referenda that were held?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. The Croatian police did not intervene because it had instructions not to aggravate inter-ethnic tensions, because these referenda were illegal anyway and did not carry any force of law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the police disturb the work of the SDS party before the war?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Never, either of the SDS or other parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your police station ever receive an instruction to arrest or even kill radical Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: On the contrary. Instructions always came in to act in a pacifying manner, in a tolerant manner, to engage in conversation rather than any other means, because the expectation was that the situation would calm down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that such an order, that means to arrest or kill radical Serbs, was given to any other police station?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't think so. I'm not aware of any such thing, and I did not go any further. I did not go out of Slatina. As far as I know, no, there were no such instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen on the 2nd of October, 1990?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: That was the first attack against the police station. That was carried out around 1900 hours by about 800 to 1.000 militant Serbs who were armed and who had assembled in Slatina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who organised this gathering in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: According to what we saw, it was the top people of the Serb Democratic Party that brought the masses there. They were headed by Milun Karadzic, then Ilija Sasic, Momcilo Subotic, and other top people from those ranks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that it was an attack on the police station. What did those gathering there want to do? What did they want?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They wanted to enter the police station at any cost, to obtain the weapons from there and to establish their own government in Slatina. This attack took place after the police station in Knin had been taken over. Also, some police stations in Banija. The station in Petrinja had already been attacked. Also in Pakrac. And right after the attack on the police station in Pakrac, this attack on the police station in Slatina took place. So the objective was to take over the police station, to seize the weapons, and to establish government there. And the ultimate objective was to cut the Podravina road and also to cut off Eastern Slavonia in this way from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did they actually say such things or how do you know?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, that was quite clear from the actual chronology of the events concerned. Knin, Banija, Petrinja, Pakrac, all of this was along this imagined corridor of Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica where the border was actually supposed to be, the border of a Greater Serbia, or as it was said then, of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when this happened in the police station?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. I led the defence of the police station. I engaged about 20 policemen who were ethnic Croats, there were also Serbs who at that time still accepted Croatian authority, and with a great deal of effort, we did manage to defend the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with these Serbian -- the leaders of the SDS that were present? And if so, what did they say?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The leaders of the SDS did have contact with me because I was at the entrance into the police station. However, they went to speak to the chief of the police station, Kresimir Libl. Afterwards, I found out that they had come to stop weapons from being taken from the police station because they were afraid that the weapons would not be taken. And at that time at the police station, we had 150 rifles for the reserve force and for the active force. All the weapons were there, and there was no need to attack the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you can explain something to me. From the transcript, I see that you said, "I found out that they had come to stop weapons from being taken from the police station." Who came to stop weapons being taken from the police station?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, according to the claims of the leadership of the SDS, they came to do that, and citizens did, although we did not expect an attack on the police station. I don't see why 1.000 armed citizens would attack the police station and ask for weapons from the police station. And of course, according to the actual establishment, these weapons belonged to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you -- you could defend the police station. Was there actually a fight, or how did you defend the police station?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: We placed a cordon of policemen in front of the police station, and they prevented the masses from entering the police station. At that moment, Mato Mesaros came through this crowd. He was in his own car and the masses were beating his car and shouting at him, and it was very hard for him to get through this crowd because he was in a hurry to pick up his wife from the health centre.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We do not need so many details. Was anyone hurt? Was anyone hurt while this incident took place? And don't describe all the details, please.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: When this citizen was returning with his car again through the crowd, his car was overturned. He was stabbed. He was wounded. His stomach was cut so his intestines spilled out onto the road. We made an ultimate effort to save his life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This violent incident, did it actually bring the matter to an end?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. After we escorted the wounded man to hospital, in front of the building, the top people of the SDS were making speeches. Again they were flagrantly insulting the Croatian state, the Croatian people, they were inciting violence. And as the masses were dispersing, they fired hundreds of gunshots into the air and in this way disturbed law and order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a JNA barracks in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, right by the police station. And it was about 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While this incident occurred while there was this attacking, did the JNA ever intervene and try to stop the crowd?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: At that time, the JNA did not intervene. On the 4th of August, 1991, they attacked us, though, with heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We come to this later. At -- you mentioned already that at that time the police force in Slatina was mixed Croats and Serbs. Did this composition change after the events that you just described?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, until that event at the police station in Slatina, about 80 to 85 per cent were Serbs and the rest were Croats. Immediately after this event, part of the policemen who were ethnic Serbs started leaving the Croatian police. The Ministry of the Interior, of course, started manning the station with other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb policemen leave on their own or were they dismissed?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Quite voluntarily. Nobody was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did these policemen go? What did they do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: At first they went to their homes; and later on, when reservists who were ethnic Serbs were getting weapons - and that started in April 1991 in the area where the insurgency was - then everybody joined these paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any observations regarding the arming of these -- of the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: We noticed, as I've already said, that as of April 1991, the Serb Democratic Party or, rather, the JNA, started training and arming the Serb population or, rather, the reservists. They called them up into the barracks in Slatina and Nasice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all males called in for military training or only Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Only Serbs were called up. Mostly those who had undergone reserve officers' training in the former JNA, those who had a commission and those who could organise and man units. Not a single Croat was called up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the JNA also armed Serbs. What -- what did you notice to this effect? How did they do that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Those who completed their training at the barracks in Slatina and Nasice immediately went to the area where the insurgency was, with their weapons, and in the month of June, from the barracks in Nasice, the police had received instructions to escort a convoy of over 40 trucks that were loaded with weapons from Nasice to Mikleus. And then further on, the police could not go any further, they could only take the highway. After that, the convoy of the JNA with weapons went to where the insurgency was, towards Vocin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me clarify. This convoy with weapons, did this convoy come from a barracks or where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: From the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it go to another barracks or where?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. It headed to the area where the insurgency was that was later organised by the Serbs. That is to say, towards Vocin and towards Sekulinci, where the weapons were unloaded. And the same night, they started distributing weapons to the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: That was in the month of June 1991. A Serb who did not want to accept a weapon, when he went to Slatina, when he tried to report that to the police, he was killed by the cemetery in Ceralije, and the police from Slatina was there to carry out the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you, the police, had to escort this weapon convoy, and you said you only were on the road and later could not follow. Why not?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, this convoy was escorted by the police from Nasice, by a police escort from Nasice. And they were in a position to do so only to the petrol station in Mikleus where the road starts that leads to the area Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that was occupied later. The policemen who were in this escort reported to us later that members of the JNA stopped them there and gave them the following orders: That they would not be allowed to escort the convoy any further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the -- did you see the convoy return?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I did not see the convoy return. However, I did see the report that said that the convoy returned the same evening and that the load remained at the area where the insurgency was?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness the Exhibit 327, tab 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is this? Is this a --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is an exhibit that we used already with the Witness C-037, and this witness will be asked a few additional questions that the previous witness was not able to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we have exhibits in these large bundles, given the logistics here, it's very difficult for us to get to them. So -- it's difficult for us to get them, so we need copies if you're going to refer backwards and forwards out of the bundle. Is it in a new bundle, do I understand?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have it in the witness binder. Just use the Exhibit number that it has now been assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not get into a muddle. This is in -- you have exhibited, re-exhibited here. It will be removed in due course from this particular binder. In due course, we will get on to the witness -- the binder of this particular witness, but let's deal with the exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after you -- these documents -- these documents, do you know them? Have you seen that before?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I know these documents. They were found at the command of the paramilitary units at Zvecevo after the units withdrew between the 12th and the 13th -- or, rather, on the 14th of December, 1991. I think that these documents were found there, as well as other documents, and they show the entire establishment of the so-called Territorial Defence, all the units involved, the Papuk detachment, and the lower-level units within.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is becoming totally senseless. We've crossed the line of absurdity with these exhibits. An attempt is being made to tender a document here that was compiled in the Virovitica Podravina police administration, the third police station of the Croatian authorities, and it says "List of Serbo-terrorist Unit Members." This is not a document at all. It cannot be treated as a document. It is not a list that could have been found at some places, let's put it this way, where these Chetniks that he's referring to left them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can make these points when you come to cross-examine. We've dealt before with this particular issue of documents, and in fact we've dealt with this document or, rather, the binder this document came out of, when we dealt with the last witness. As we've told you, we admit documents here as hearsay. We decide what weight to give them. Now, the point which you appear to be making about this one is that it refers to members of a Serbo or something terrorist units. Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, isn't it clear to you that this kind of document could not be found any Serb office, as the witness put it and the way this is being introduced here? Can't you see that this is a Croatian document? After all, this is no document. Even a police document would have to have a date and a signature. It is not a document at all. This is no document. These are simply two sheets of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a challenge to the authenticity of the documents. It's already been admitted, of course, by the last witness. Just -- don't interrupt. It's already been admitted. You've heard the challenge, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. It's a matter for you to deal with it. It's said it's plainly a Croat document from the heading, and, therefore, it may be not of particular use to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to speak about this document with the witness because he dealt with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us hear about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that these documents were found in Zvecevo, and you said it was on the -- after the withdrawal. When were these documents found; in which year?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, let's settle the dilemma. The first two pieces of paper are merely a list, a list of documents and units. The rest are photocopies of original documents. Therefore, it is true that this is a list which was compiled by the police, and all the rest are original documents or, rather, photocopies of them. Those and numerous other documents were found, as I've already said, in the command, the headquarters of Zvecevo, after the area was placed under the control of the Croatian army. And from this, it is clearly evident how the Papuk detachment was set up and all the others were established, with their concrete duties, assignments, names - first names, last names - the types and numbers of the weapons. And in addition to these documents, I've already said we also found many others. Let me also mention that the command headquarters and the entire recreational centre, once these units had withdrawn, were set fire to and completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who found the documents, the police or another body?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian army found them. And then later on, they were handed over to the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your work as a police officer, did you have to handle these documents? What did you do with it?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: All those documents, along with the notifications sent to the District Court and public prosecutor were sent as reports, files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you look at the first --

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They were attachments to criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you look at the first two pages, who compiled these pages?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I can't see from this because there's no signature. Probably somebody in the third police station, which later on processed these documents and looked into the case and sent in the documents to the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you look at the then following documents, they all have a stamp on there, a Croatian stamp. Do you know who made this stamp?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The stamp was placed by the officer completing the case in the files and it was placed there in order to authenticate it because they were photocopies. So to show that they corresponded to the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the place Zvecevo. What -- what kind of a place was it? Was it a headquarters? Was it a JNA post? What was it?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The Zvecevo location was made up of a number of hotels owned by the Rade Koncar enterprise from Zagreb, and it had all the necessary attending facilities for sport and recreation. The members of the paramilitary units and the Papuk detachment took it over and set up its command headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "paramilitary units," what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, I mean the Papuk detachment which was established following the 12th Slavonia Shock Brigade that was a participant of the war -- during World War II, and all the subsequent units that were under the Papuk detachment and which made up the so-called Territorial Defence, which was not actually Territorial Defence because the Republic of Croatia had its own Territorial Defence and the established formations that were inherited from the former Yugoslavia and whose weapons it had -- whose weapons had been confiscated by the JNA because that -- those weapons were stored in the warehouses of the JNA, and the army gave the weapons to the rebel Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Where can we find this Zvecevo headquarters, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness -- it's actually the map Exhibit C338.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit 325.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is already -- it's already in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 325. MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put it on the ELMO and actually point out where Zvecevo is? You have to look at the map, not on the screen, sir.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness is pointing at the place with his finger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's described as Novo Zvecevo on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we are already with the map, can you point out where Vocin is.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And what is the distance between Zvecevo and Vocin, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: About 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That is enough with the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall when this Zvecevo place, when it started to function as a post of the Serbian TO?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: While that area was under the control of the rebel Serbs, throughout that time, Zvecevo was the centre of the command and the headquarters, right up until the 14th of December, 1991, until it was placed under the control of the Croatian army. Otherwise, this area was under the temporary occupation, that is to say from the 18th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We do not need to go into all the details of the structure of the TO because there is no time to do that. I would like to address just a few documents from this exhibit. The first one is actually document number 57 in the index list and also marked accordingly on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, can I just go through this. We must produce these exhibits in an orderly way. Yes. You must introduce them to us. Invite us to -- you want us to look at this bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And there is an index on top of it, and the index actually has numbers, number 1 to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Attachment numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, attachment numbers. And you'll find those same numbers in the documents, both in the translation and in the B/C/S. So if you follow simply those numbers which are in -- which are on top --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have that, of course. We can see that. But in each case, when you produce a new bundle or a new exhibit, we must pause while a number is assigned to it. You have your numbers, your Prosecution reference numbers. These are of no use to the Court. They may be of use to you and helpful for you to find your way around, but obviously, once a document is exhibited, it must be referred to by the court number. Now, we'll have an exhibit number for this particular bundle now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The registrar seems to think we have given this an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If so, then it has completely eluded me. When did we give this a number? What was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Kindly explain the position to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, this document was discussed already with the witness 37 and on this occasion got Exhibit number, the court Exhibit number 372, tab 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've dealt with that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And this document contains a lot of documents, and internally this document has got an index number according to the index on top of the document. And when I refer to a number 57 or 58, it's meant just the order of this document. It's not another exhibit or not another exhibit number to be assigned, just help to find your way through that extensive document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So is this all Exhibit 327, tab 13?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again. Right. Now we have it. Could you, before you begin with this sort of exhibit, just explain to the Court what you're up to and then we will be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the index list, if you find the -- mentioned the attachment 57, and in the index, it says, "Unit command and members of the Zvecevo unit." It's the English translation of the index list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For my part, I can't find an attachment 57 or where it is. I just have a single sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You'll find it. Just keep going through the bundle, you'll come to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's after the extensive list of names. To assist you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, we're in early days of this part of the case so we need to get these things right. For a start, it is misleading to say it's exhibit to be tendered through Mr. Matovina, as it's headed here, when in fact it's an old exhibit, as it transpires. So once we have an exhibit, refer to it always by the exhibit designation. The other point is that in the other parts of the case, we've had numbered dividers, I suppose you would call them, as opposed to these attachments, which is very difficult to see as you go through. I mean, you can find 57 simply by going through it, but if you can have the dividers with the numbers, it would be much easier for us to find our way round it. And as I say, once you've got an exhibit number for it, always refer to it by that exhibit number and then there will be less confusion. Mr. Kay, have you got 57?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I've worked it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at this document -- the document 57, it refers here to the municipal staff of Slovanska Pozega, Zvecevo detachment, and it refers to -- it says here: "For your further use, attached find a list of fighters, detachment Slovanska Pozega municipal staff, support technical staff in the Zvecevo facility." Who signs it, do you know, for the commander?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The signature is the commander's, Commander Munja, and on the list it says that it is Commander Borivoj Lukic, Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, are you recognising the name by his signature in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging by the signature on the attached document, no, but this document clearly shows that the accompanying document and the principal document were signed by one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by saying that, you refer to the list attached to this document which is also signed, or what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. On the list, we see the same signature as we do on the attached document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is referring to the list attached to this cover letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who is Munja? Is that a proper name?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: It's a pseudonym, and I think that under the name Munja was the person of Commander Borivoj Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, I think that through the other lists, although 11 years has gone by since that time, that pseudonym cropped up. However, in some other documents, we also found that Veljko Vukelic would sign himself using the nickname Munja, or pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that at that time or how did you learn about this fact that Mr. Vukelic also operated under "Munja"?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Later on, from the numerous witness statements that were given after that area was placed under the control of the Croatian authorities and when this whole case of the armed uprising was discussed, then people in their statements did mention Veljko Vukelic and he was to be found in the documents as well. He was one of the leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party for Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I think I've found the name Munja on page 12 of 17 in the English translation, and I could find it in the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, looking at the list of fighters, you have as the first person here Commander Borivoj Lukic, Captain First Class. Is that the Mr. Lukic that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's the captain. He was in command of that detachment, the Zvecevo detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Boro Lukic, who was he? Was he a JNA person? Was he a local person? Can you tell us something about him?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: He was born in Vocin. After the -- before the war, he was a maintenance man for the machinery in the Gaj Slatina enterprise. He completed the school for reserve officers and had the rank of captain first class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he an SDS member? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: He joined the SDS in its very first days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I've known -- I've worked with him -- I worked with him for a number of years in the Gaj enterprise, and I know him personally from our day-to-day meetings. We would see each other on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his attitude towards Croats? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: He was an Orthodox. He was intolerant, and he was among the first to leave Slatina. First of all, he went to the Sekulinci stock where the infrastructure existed for training the reserve members of the army, reserve soldiers. We knew about that because he was out of town for quite some time. And whenever a reservist would leave, we knew that they were leaving in fact to join his detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you -- what information did you get that he was the commander? Did you know it at that time already or just through these documents?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: We knew this straight away, as soon as he left. And at that time -- I think it was May 1991, in fact. As I say, at that time, we still communicated with that area which was later under provisional occupation so that we learnt that he was training people up there. They said he was training the Territorial Defence members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These other people that are listed on -- as fighters and -- on this list attached to the document we are discussing, were you aware at that time that they had these positions? Could you help us if that is a correct picture of the TO structure?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that was the correct picture of the TO structure. We knew about some of the people and we learnt of others later on, once the documents had been uncovered. But quite a number of people from this list I know personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like now to turn to the last document that is in this bundle named 57. If you just turn the pages, you come to a document dated 5 November 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it in attachment 57, is it, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. I just heard that this is actually a document related -- it's numbered 58. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I had it misplaced in my version. It's a document with the number 58 on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this is a document, an authorisation dated the 5th November 1991, signed by Munja, and there is a handwritten remark on it saying, "Veljko Vukelic is the one hiding behind Munja." Do you know how this handwritten note came onto the document?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: That's what I was talking about a moment ago, that I had seen somewhere in the documents this kind of note. And this was probably written in by one of the duty officers because there were a number of officers working on the case, and when in talking to the witnesses and those who had taken part in the uprising, they learnt that behind "Munja" was the person whose name was Veljko Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this handwritten note was then written, if I understand you correctly, by a Croat policeman and was not on the original when it was found.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. This was written after the knowledge that we had amassed, the information that we -- had been collected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Veljko Vukelic, is he from Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, he's also from Slatina. He was the secretary of the committee of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and just before the war, he was Secretary for National Defence in Slatina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The duties of the Secretary of National Defence, what was it? What did that include?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, the Secretary of National Defence keeps the records of all recruits and sends out newcomers to do their military training. Reservists are called up. That is one of the duties of the secretariat, to call them up for additional training - they are sent to schools for reserve officers - and they have an overall insight into matters of this kind, all the civil matters with respect to defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time is now half past; time for the adjournment. We're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Mr. Matovina, would you please bear in mind not to speak to anyone about your evidence until it's over during these adjournments, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Would you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, we were speaking about Mr. Vukelic and actually about his position as the Secretary of the Defence -- the National Defence department in Slatina. As a secretary in this position, would he have to work with -- closely with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, he had very close ties to the JNA and cooperated with them very closely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of this position or -- I mean, what do you mean? The duty, the duties of a Secretary of Defence, National Defence, does that include close work and cooperation with the JNA or not?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Precisely. His duties included this cooperation, and as far as I could see, his ties with them were very close and his cooperation was on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Secretary of National Defence in a municipality, would he have working relations with federal organs or republican organs in his work?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, the secretary had ties strictly with the republican organs and through them received instructions from the federal organs and carried out the policies of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Vukelic was in this position as secretary before the war. When did he leave this position? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in April 1991, in the very first days of armed insurgency or, rather, the distribution of weapons to the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what position he took after he left Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that he went to Western Slavonia and that he was one of the leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party, which was in charge of all these affairs, including the arming of the population, establishment of units, and the entire armed insurgency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document that we just discussed where there is this handwritten remark on it referring to Mr. Vukelic, it is a document, as we saw, from the municipal staff Slavonska Pozega. Is this place Zvecevo in the municipality of Slovanska Pozega?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. It is part of Slavonska Pozega in territorial terms, but this area is closely interlinked by communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I want to put the geographic data more visible to you. We have a municipality map. The problem with this municipality map - we have copies for everyone - but we have reduced it to a format that you can see the municipalities clearly but not so much -- you have to have eagle eyes to see the villages. We have the huge map for purposes here in the courtroom, and we will also provide you all with a huge map but we don't have it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At the moment, we have only the small one, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for you to see the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see those. Let's give it an exhibit number before we move on. This is both Croatia, is it right, and also Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 333.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually, the big -- for the usher, the huge format has to be put on the ELMO. And I can fold it for you so that you have the right part in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you point out to us the two municipalities we spoke about, that is, Slatina and Pozega. On the map, please, not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at the municipality Pozega. And now can you turn the map a little bit down. Yes. And now the witness is pointing at the municipality Slatina.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And could the focus be so that we can more clear -- see more clearly. Focusing on the two municipalities, please. Yes. And can you now point out to us -- yes. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now point out to us where Zvecevo was? Zvecevo where we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is pointing at the -- almost at the border between the two municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now Vocin. Vocin, please.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at Vocin. And you also mentioned a place Sekulinci. Could you show us Sekulinci?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's enough. Thank you. Witness, speaking of Sekulinci, do you know what was in Sekulinci during the war?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: During the war and during the temporary occupation of that area, in this depot of Sekulinci, in this area of Sekulinci, there was a camp through which dozens of Croats passed. They were tortured there, mistreated, and two of them were killed, their corpses later found in a clearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that? What is your information on this?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: There are witness statements from people who had been kept there, tortured, detained for ten days to two months, and we have a statement from one female witness who had been kept there in a metal container, tortured and raped repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get this information in your work as a police officer? Were you involved in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, through the interviews conducted with people who had been detained in those camps and who had managed to survive and reach the free territory. And there were also people who had been exchanged during that temporary occupation. They were exchanged for people from territories under the control of Croatian authorities. Those were mainly kinsmen of high-ranking commanders, and they were exchanged for people, detainees, from the Sekulinci camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time did this Sekulinci camp exist?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the occupation of that area, that is from the 18th of August, 1991, until the territory came under the control of Croatian authorities. The commander was Zoran Miscevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you speak to witnesses and when did you conduct the investigation? At what time?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Back in the time when this territory was not under Croatian control, we talked to people who had come from the area of Vocin after an exchange. And after the liberation of this area, all the surviving detainees gave statements, and they are still on record, on file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understand you, that's December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, December 1991. But not only. There are statements dating back to earlier times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning back to the document that -- the exhibit that we are discussing, I would like to move to the exhibits belonging to attachment 58. It's a list of volunteers of Serbian Radical Party going on leave from the 9th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in terms of the proofing summary, what paragraph are we in, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are in the document -- in the paragraph 21 and 22, actually. TO formations. It's all TO formations, and we are speaking about the Papuk detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we haven't gone far, to paragraph 29 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Kwon, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't gone far, to paragraph 29, which the witness stated just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Sekulinci. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We're still dealing with the TO formation, as it is in 20 to 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this list of -- this list of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party is signed by a person, Rajko Bojcic. Do you know this person and his position during the war?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I know Rajko Bojcic personally. He was assistant to Boro Lukic. He has signed here as the commander of the municipal staff of Territorial Defence. Otherwise, he used to be a teacher by occupation who worked in Slatina. However, in the first days of the insurgency, he left for the area where the units of the so-called Territorial Defence were set up, and he served as assistant to Boro Lukic, commander of the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were in the region of Podravska Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: We became aware of that towards the end of October 1991 when some persons were exchanged from the territory under occupation. More precisely, they came to Slatina after being exchanged. Those people were Croats who had remained up there when the area was cut off from Slatina, and the other territory under Croatian control. These persons confirmed for us that towards the end of October, volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party arrived in Vocin. They were so-called White Eagles. There were about 300 to 400 of them. Some witness statements even mentioned a figure of 600. Several people said, however, that they were 300 to 400.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see those volunteers arrive or leave or in between?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: That was 25 kilometres away from Slatina. We had no way of knowing what was going on in the area. However, eyewitnesses confirmed that these volunteers left the area on six buses towards the end of occupation, and these 300 or 400 volunteers were the last to leave after that massacre in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there -- are you aware that any other volunteer groups than those from the Serbian Radical Party were in Slatina? Any other volunteers from Serbia than those?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I know nothing about any other groups. I know only about this one for which I have a partial list which was found together with other documents in the command headquarters in Zvecevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as the last document from this row of -- from this exhibit, I would like to turn to the exhibit that is marked as attachment 60. Witness, I just want you to have a look at the person signing this document. Do you know this person? Can you tell us who signs it and what his position was?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: We see here the signature of the command of the area staff of Territorial Defence, and judging by some other signatures, I believe this is the signature of Boro Radosavljevic, who was also one of the SDS leaders and at the very top of the military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. He too was a reserve officer of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can now leave this document, Your Honour. This is actually all I wanted to discuss in relation to this document with the witness. Just for your reference, when you look at number 62, the attachment number 62, you see actually the same -- one of the documents shows the full name of the person we just discussed, Boro Radosavljevic. With the help of the usher, I would like to address with the witness briefly the exhibit - and this is now a new exhibit not yet introduced - it's Exhibit 2775, and it would need -- it's tab 2 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How are we going to exhibit the remainder of this witness's exhibits? There seem to be, is it right, another ten exhibits to go --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff? Would you like those exhibited together as a separate number and then various tabs within it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll get the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 334.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this document is a note of the Virovitica Podravina police administration listing several documents, and if you look at the last two items, they refer to documents -- refer to volunteers from Serbia, a list of volunteers from Serbia. Those documents are signed by police officers. Do you know whether these police officers were working in the police station and dealt with these particular items?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. We see the signatures of police officers Miroslav Gumbarevic and commander Mirko Kostelac. The former was on this case from the very beginning, and the list contains an overview of all documents that were made available to the investigators of this Tribunal. The date indicated is the 22nd February 2001, when I was no longer working in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just submit this document to show how we got it, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now move to the next document in the binder, and it is the Prosecution Exhibit C4328, and it's tab 3 in the binder. Witness, this is a report on the TO staff of Western Slavonia, and I would like you to look at the entries related to the municipal staff of Podravska Slatina. And we find here Boro Radosavljevic, whom you just mentioned, and there is also another person. Do you know -- can you tell us the name -- the correct spelling of this person, this second person listed as commander?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The name of this second person is Dragomir Keleuva, K-E-L-E-U-V-A. He worked in the defence secretariat of Slatina, and he too left for the insurgent area at the very outset and carried out various duties, such as commander of the battalion, as we see here. Generally speaking, he was an expert in communications, radio devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all in relation to this document. And we would have to have a -- oh, it's part of the bundle. Sorry. Witness, did -- do you -- do you know a person, an officer, Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No, I don't know him. I know he is a colonel of the JNA who arrived in the insurgent area from Novi Sad accompanied by an officer by the name of Simic with a task of consolidating the defence and, as a military expert, strengthening the military component of the units that had been established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how -- what information did you get in this regard? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Again, through interviews with people from Vocin who know Colonel Trbojevic personally because he is originally from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned earlier, in the beginning, actually, of your testimony, you mentioned that the JNA attacked the Slatina police station. When did that happen and what happened?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: That second attack on the police station in Slatina happened on the 4th of August, 1991, around 2300 hours. From the barracks, 50 kilometres away from the police station, the JNA used heavy weaponry and two BOV armoured vehicles to attack the premises where a transition of duties was being carried out. However, this ceremony took part a little earlier, thus avoiding a catastrophe, because there would have been dozens of dead policemen if the transition of duties took place just a little later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the police officers or -- yes. Did the police officers Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. provoke this JNA attack? Had they done something before that could have provoked them?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The attack was not provoked. The attack was not expected either, although for days the guns of the armoured vehicles were aimed at the police station from inside the barracks. The policemen from the police station went to their regular preventive duties in town, and from the nearby hill that was already under the control of the insurgents, several shells were fired at the police station and the military barracks. So in that way, the attack was provoked. The objective of this attack was for it to take place exactly at 2300 hours when the transition of duty takes place, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've told us that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when the largest number of policemen are present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just clarify something. You said that from the nearby hill there was firing at the police station and the military barracks. Who did that; Croats?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. This was done by the rebel Serbs who came to that area. Later on, we obtained the exact names of the persons who had done that, because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We would not need the details. Thank you. Did the JNA ever take over Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the JNA barracks in Slatina? Was it taken over by the Croats at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: After this incident, it became clear that the JNA did not have good intentions vis-a-vis the police and the people in town, the town where they had lived until then without any problems whatsoever. As for the members of the Croatian army, a few days later, they carried out a blockade of the military barracks. And on the 16th of September, the military barracks were handed over to the Croatian army without any fighting and without any casualties or anything. This was done in a peaceful way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the JNA then leave Slatina, those in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, members of the JNA who were doing their military service were allowed to go home. The officers were also released. One of them actually returned on the following day and said that he had forgotten his pistol, and he went looking for it in the barracks. After that day, there was no more JNA in Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to have put to the witness again the Exhibit 338, the map with the red zone. Witness, this region -- this part of the map that is indicated in red, is that the territory that the Serbs controlled during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we don't follow the number 338.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Prosecutor's Exhibit 326, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. I used the old --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at this red zone, is that the territory that was controlled by the Serbs during the war at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The area is properly marked on the map. That is the area concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the Serbs take over this territory? Did they really fight their way into it?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. After they armed the population, after they made sure that they had a proper military establishment, they placed roadblocks on all the roads leading to that area. Quite simply, they did not allow the institutions of Croatian government to function there any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Croatian authorities try to get it back with force?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: In the period during which the area was under temporary occupation, there were several initiatives of the Croatian authorities for this area to be integrated peacefully into the constitutional system of the Republic of Croatia. Certain people went there, messages were dispatched, and every effort was made to resolve the problem by peaceful means. However, the Serb insurgents did not agree to this at all, although people were aware that most of the population would have agreed to it. However, military groups and the military establishment did not allow this at all. So after the massacres in Cetekovac and Vocin were carried out and after all the crimes they had committed between the 12th and the 13th of December, 1991, these units indeed forced the population to act according to their wishes. So together with the population, they withdrew to the Pozega-Kamensko-Pakrac line where, afterwards, the UN protected area was established. So this was the area in the direction of the Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you here, and let's turn to the Exhibit C2685, and it is tab 4 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Prosecution Exhibit 334.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this is an investigative file related to a massacre that you just referred to. You mentioned already Cetekovac, and I would like to discuss a few details from this file. Did you yourself deal with this incident in Cetekovac, Balinci, and Cojlug?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.
