I personally coordinated the activities of the officials who worked on collecting the information and evidence connected to this first major massacre that was carried out at the very outset of the insurgency of a certain portion of the Serb population. I was at the actual scene of the massacre. I saw the victims. I took part in retrieving their bodies and compiling all the information needed for this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these villages Cetekovac, Balinci and Cojlug, were these Croatian villages?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Cetekovac was purely a Croat village. As for Cojlug and Balinci, the population was mixed. All three villages are practically interconnected and they are all along the road that leads to Vocin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the massacre happen?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The massacre happened on the 4th of September, 1991, around 9.00, in all three of these villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Croatian military forces in these villages?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. There were only civilians there. As for the persons killed, there were two policemen who happened to be in the village then because it was their day off, and they were from that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Twenty-two civilians were killed and two policemen. This number includes three women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they killed?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They were killed by firearms from close range. There were victims who were stabbed by knives as well. Most of the corpses were massacred later, and two bodies were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your investigative file, you have listed the 24 victims, and you also list a lot of perpetrators. To which unit did those identified perpetrators belong? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: This was the first charge sheet that was filed after the massacre. These are members of a special platoon that operated within the Papuk detachment. It is actually -- the number involved is actually larger, but this was the first information that we had obtained when talking to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were actually on the scene and present and saw bodies. Were the villages also destroyed? Do you know that? Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Most of the houses were torched and blown up. Houses were shot at from heavy weapons, mortars. In Cetekovac, practically half of the village and even more was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether JNA soldiers were involved in this attack?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. As far as we know, the JNA did not take part in this attack. It was only the local people, including those from the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now move on to Vocin. Did you investigate the -- what happened in Vocin as well?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I was involved in the coordination of the activities of some 20 officials who were engaged in this case, because this was a rather large-scale task, and it came just after the area was brought under Croatian control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a Croatian village or was it a mixed village?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Vocin was a mixed village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Croats leave this village when it came under control, under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: A smaller number of Croats were forced to stay up there. Actually, they could not leave the area. During the occupation, a number left the area either illegally or through exchanges. Otherwise, for the most part, there were Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, before going too far, it's about the events in Cetekovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are in Vocin, but before we go too far. Are those events included in the indictment? You said -- according to the summary, it's crime base, but could you clarify that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Cetekovac is not included in the indictment as a charge, I only refer to this incident with the witness to describe that there was a widespread systematic attack occurring in various places. Therefore, I also did not go into many details. The crime base is actually Vocin, and we will speak now about Vocin and then can actually conclude this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Croats were forced to stay. How were they forced to stay?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't leave the area because all communications were under the control of armed Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they not allowed to leave? Did someone force them to stay and not let them out?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. On the day when the police station in Vocin was taken by the rebel Serbs, that is to say the 19th of August, 1991, all Croats were gathered in one place from the streets where they predominantly lived in Vocin and beyond, and they were told that from then on, they had to recognise the authority of the SAO Krajina, that the regulations of the Croatian state were no longer in force and that they had to remain in the area of Vocin, where they were given work duty. Because in addition to the military authorities there, there was also the civilian authorities that had been established too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that some Croats left illegally. What do you mean by they left "illegally"?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, during the night, they got into the woods and came to Slatina where they testified about all the terrible things that happened up there during the temporary occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened up there? What did -- what was done to the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The day the police station was taken, all Croats who had weapons with permits, that is to say hunting guns, pistols that they had had from earlier on, all these weapons were taken away from them. Their houses were searched. They were looking for about 50 rifles with which they had allegedly been armed by the Croatian authorities. They were shooting at these people's houses. They were intimidated, and there was systematic mistreatment. Individuals were taken to Sekulinci camp. They were mistreated there, beaten. Some persons even went missing. Until the present day, six persons from that area are missing. No one knows where they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness the Exhibit C2684, and it is tab 6 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Prosecutor's Exhibit 334.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned -- you just mentioned Sekulinci camp, and this is a document related to a person -- medical document, actually, related to a victim Mr. Zdravko Volf. Did you have dealings with this victim Mr. Volf?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. I have a document of Darko Bozickovic, a policeman, that's what I have here in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was an accompanying person.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, sorry. Yes. Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about this case, that the patient was beaten on the 22nd of August in Sekulinci and Macute? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, this is policeman Darko Bozickovic. Zoran Miscevic took him to Sekulinci, and over there he was beaten up, tortured, and then released. Subsequently, he joined the Croatian police in Slatina. He is one of the four policemen who were Croats who, when the police station in Vocin was taken over, was disarmed and then they were expelled from the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Want the help of the usher, I would like now to put to the witness the Exhibit C2687.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In tab 6, I only have a list with four names on it, of four local persons from Slatina and who were sent to the JNA. I don't have any of the documents that the other side is referring to. In the case of the previous witness, I had some documents that were completely different, not the ones that the other side was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll make sure you got a copy. Between now and the adjournment, between now and the adjournment, Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff, could you make sure the accused has a copy of tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic has, actually, the documents but they are, unfortunately, in a different order given to him. So I'm sorry. I just hear that. He has -- the reason for this is that the -- he got the exhibits in advance, and actually when I prepared for this testimony, I slightly changed the order and it was, unfortunately, not reflected. The accused actually has it, but we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can't find it if it's in a wrong place. Could you make sure he gets a copy in the same order as we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And if on any occasion you give us exhibits in a different order, you might as well give him a copy too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The problem arose actually on the weekend when we found out that Mr. Samardzic could not come, and therefore we could not adjust the documents for the accused. So today is a little bit out of the usual. However, I would like now to turn to the document C2687, and it's tab 7. And to assist Mr. Milosevic, we are actually speaking about three medical documents related to Vocin. They should be one after the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have here a document related to a victim Antun Simic, and it says that he was beaten on the 19th of August, 1991, in Vocin. Are you aware of this incident?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I know Antun Simic personally, and I know exactly when this incident took place. He was one of the people who managed to get away from the occupied area by taking to the woods, and he saved his life in that way. But he has serious and lasting adverse effects from the beating, and he now feels all those adverse effects from everything that he lived through at the Sekulinci camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like now to put the document 2688, and that's tab number 8, to the witness. And it refers to a victim, Kresimir Doric, who, as it says on the document, was beaten up on the 29th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of this incident?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I am. There is a statement by Kresimir Doric pertaining to the event which took place on the 29th of August, 1991. And here we have the medical records as well. He is in Slatina today. He's working there as a driver, and he also suffered adverse effects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the Vocin massacre. When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The massacre happened between the 12th and 13th of December, 1991, which is to say the last day that the rebel Serbs held the area under their control, as well as the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who -- what happened and who did it?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, when the withdrawal took place, the special purposes unit of the most extreme group of men, and according to the witnesses they say between 60 and 80 of the White Eagle members were with them, and they perpetrated the massacre of the civilian population. And to all intents and purposes, they destroyed the whole of Vocin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mention "White Eagles," what does it mean? Is that the unit -- is that what we spoke about before, volunteers of the SRS party, or is this another group?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. They were the volunteers that we mentioned earlier on. It was a group of men which was set up together with the special purposes unit, and they carried out that massacre in Vocin. Another larger group one day -- one or two days before that, had left the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many persons were killed?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: According to what we were able to establish on the basis of documents, because the massacre was not carried out only in Vocin but there were massacres in a number of localities around Vocin, the total number of people killed was 45, and most of them or, rather, all of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you bring your investigative file with you when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. I brought my notes with me, and I can explain the other localities where massacres took place apart from the one in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did not have this investigative file beforehand. The witness brought it with him. And we do not intend to tender it because it's not translated, but I think it would be helpful if the witness could use his file so that we just can go through the names of the victims as they are in the indictment. It would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- probably assist him if he could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And do we have it exhibited at tab 9 of whatever it is, Exhibit 334?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because we didn't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What have we got at tab 9, since I've got it open?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tab 9 is actually the people who were expelled from Vocin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We do not have the file and also not the list of victims. What we want to exhibit here is actually the annex to the indictment. This is what we would like to become an exhibit, because we have on this -- in this annex, we have the names of the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If the witness can confirm it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to be put to the witness the Annex I of the indictment with the list of victims from Vocin. And at the same time, I would ask Your Honours to allow him to consult his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, if they were notes made at the time. Were these notes part of the investigation, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those notes were part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can refer to them when you're giving this part of the evidence. And Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we must have a copy, please, in due course, of this exhibit for our files.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And we actually have provided a copy of this investigative file to Mr. Milosevic so that he can follow. We just didn't want to enter it because it's not translated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can use your file, sir. Mr. Matovina, you can use your investigative file that you have with you.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On number -- on pages 20 to 22, you have a list of victims. Just look at this. And it's also a help for Mr. Milosevic, it's on page 20 and the following two. And let us look at Annex I of the indictment. Could you confirm that those listed in the Prosecution annex, if you go through the names, are these names --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. In what you've just provided me with, I have under this tab just seven pages with a list of individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Coming up is the list. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go through the list from the first name, Simic, Jaga, through to Ivankovic, Drago, were these people killed during the Vocin massacre in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I was able to count them, there are 31 victims here, 31 people who were killed in Vocin. However, when we dealt with the Vocin case, our final numbers were -- that is to say between the 12th and the 13th of December, 1991, when this massacre took place, our final count included several other locations one or two days before or perhaps on the same day when a number of people were also killed. So that in the village of Hum, for example, which is four kilometres away from Vocin, Marko Vukovic was killed, born in 1934. And then there was Djuzel Marijan. 1931 was his date of birth. Roman Ridl, born in 1932. And that body was burnt. And Ivo Banovac, born in 1934. In the village of Kraskovic on that same day when the withdrawal took place, the Kovac family was liquidated. Zlatko Kovac, born in 1966; in Djuro Kovac, born in 1922; Ana Kovac, born in 1927; and Pista Kovac, born in 1953. Then we come to Zvecevo, which is where the Slavko Perisic family was killed. He was born in 1914. And Ana Perisic, born in 1920.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about -- what about a Bokane?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: In Bokane, three bodies were found. Stojan Nenadovic was killed. He was born in 1914. He was a Serb who did not wish to leave when the rebels wanted force him to leave. And then the married couple, Tomislav Martinkovic, he was born in 1939, and Katica, his wife, was born in 1936. Their bodies were found buried in Vocina. The bodies had been buried but the heads were found in fertiliser bags and were brought to the headquarters Tutavalije [phoen] by the White Eagles, and they were handed over to the duty officer at the headquarters. His name was Ninko Djukanovic later on he testified, or rather, he's mentioned in the witness statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's turn to the annex, this annex of the indictment. When you compare this, your investigation, the list of the victims with the annex of the indictment, is the annex correct?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, the annex is correct. All I wish to mention is that the unidentified individual was thought to be like Zeljko. And later on, through the witness statements, he was in fact identified. He was a member of the Croatian army who was imprisoned at the police station in Vocin. He was held in detention there, and his body was found with handcuffs on his hands and the body was partially -- had partially been burnt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the list be exhibited. We have a copy now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Prosecutor's Exhibit 335.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just -- I'd like to ask you about two persons on the list. The first person is Branko Medic. Is that the correct spelling?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is Branko Medic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you, would you please check your own investigative file on page 20. There is a Branko Nedic, born 1959.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: It is Medic with an "M". I think it was Medic, "M," Branko and not Nedic "N."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you also have a look at Marija Matanci. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Matanci, Franjo, and Matanci, Marija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask because in your investigative file you have Marija Majdancic, born 1990. I just want to confirm, what is the correct name of the victim Marija?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Majdancic. M-A-J-D-A-N-C-I-C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That would -- this is, then, correct in the list, in the annex. Thank you. These people listed in the annex, were they civilians or are there any soldiers among them?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: All of them were civilians except Zeljko Laik who had been held in detention in Vocin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is, as you said, the unidentified person on the annex.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, at the time the list was completed, but he was identified later on as being Zeljko Laik. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The bodies, were you involved in the finding of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: After we learnt of the massacre and when the Croatian army arrived in the area, that is to say when the rebel Serbs and their units had retreated, the day after that happened, we started pulling out the dead bodies, and most of the corpses were in the houses, although some of them were outside in the open, and eyewitness identification on the spot was carried out and then post-mortems were conducted. The bodies were transferred to Slatina. Some of the bodies were taken to Osijek for the post-mortem to be held there, and I think that some of them -- for some of them, the hospital in Virovitica conducted the post-mortem examinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on from what happened in Vocin, you said in the beginning that the municipality -- you told us about the ethnic composition in the municipality. How did it change after the war?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, the war quite certainly caused migratory processes, not only in the locality of the former Slatina municipality but further afield as well. In the Slatina municipality in the throes of the war, when we were systematically bombed by JNA planes and when more than 400 shells were dropped, quite a number of refugees came into the area, about 4.000 refugees from Kosovo, expelled Croats from there, over 5.000 refugees who came in from Bosanska Posavina, and then also in Slatina a convoy of refugees were stopped which was expelled by the JNA from Ilok. Part of the refugees from Vukovar as well had to be put up in Slatina, and to add to all this, refugees from Vojvodina and Serbia turned up, Croats which were -- who were exposed to pressure there so they came to seek accommodation in Croatia. So this enormous influx, this column of refugees, remained largely in the Slatina area. And it was at that time, if I may say so, that it created a humanitarian catastrophe. This was an enormous problem, how to put up all the refugees that had come in and how to ensure that they all had a roof over their heads. After the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, just pausing there so we can understand this. These refugees were Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exclusively Croats, yes. After the war, some of the Serbs who had taken part in the armed uprising exchanged their houses for the houses of Croats who had come in from Vojvodina province. Some of them had come in from Bosnia and the Republika Srpska. Some of them sold out their properties to state agencies, and this process is still ongoing, this process of selling one's property or exchanging one's property for somebody else's, depending on where the people finally decided to stay. So these were migrations that were taking place as a result of the events that had come to pass and the war, and they without a doubt influenced the ethnic composition not only of Slatina but in the district and further afield as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I actually forgot to put one exhibit to you, and I would like to now. This is Exhibit C2691, and it is tab 9 in the binder. If you please have a look at this exhibit and tell us what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: This document refers to Croats who were refugees and had come from Vocin after the massacre was committed up there, after almost the whole of Vocin had been destroyed so that they had nowhere to live. And they came to Slatina, and this list tells us which families they were put up with until the infrastructure was set up to accommodate them and until they were able to go back to their own homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that Vocin was destroyed, the Croatian homes were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Almost entirely. The church was shelled of Our Lady of Vocin. That was shelled to the ground. And there were several tonnes of explosives released. This enormous explosion led to the destruction of hundreds of other houses where the roofs were shattered. And for example, the roof of that church was thrown two kilometres from the church itself as a result of the explosion. The whole infrastructure was destroyed; the health centre, the bus station, the fire engine department, and many, many other buildings, and Vocin resembled Hiroshima.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with one matter which I would like clarified, Mr. Matovina. You're dealing with Vocin. You said that after the Serbs withdrew, "We pulled out the bodies," and most, you said, were in the houses. Who did you mean by "we," and did it include you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was in Vocin the second day. But when I said "we," I meant the police officers, workers in the police force who went out to conduct an on-site investigation. And also the members of the Croatian army who assisted them when these bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, are you coming to an end with this witness? It's almost time for the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I actually only have one question left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it refers to your investigations. Did you file charges against persons suspected to have committed the crimes in the Vocin area and Cetekovac? And if so, what became of the charges?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: After the crime processing had been conducted and all information collected, criminal reports were filed with the District Court and prosecutor's office in Osijek, and the prosecutions in question undertook an investigation. However, most of the individuals, especially those who were involved in organising the armed uprising and indeed those who were the ringleaders of all the events that took place, were not accessible, either then or now to the Croatian courts because they are located on the territory of Serbia, Bosnia, Montenegro, et cetera. And a small number, a far smaller number of individuals who played a peripheral role in the armed uprising have been held accountable and punished, however, some of these were exchanged. So that to all intents and purposes, nobody was actually held responsible for these events. In the meantime, the Croatian Sabor, or parliament, and the Croatian state passed a law forgiving them. And most of these crimes were qualified -- they were amnestied and most of these crimes were classed as an armed uprising, and this was incorporated by the amnesty that was proclaimed. So that it was only from the area of Slatina, the former municipality of Slatina that over 1.600 people were amnestied by the law that was passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those amnestied, were the soldiers actually the TO members or were they higher ranking?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, they were members of the TO from the lists that we have just been looking at, and many of them did hold higher ranks as well. All this was shown to be a more mitigating form for purposes of tolerance. It was a gesture on the part of the state, in fact, to amnesty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We really don't want any political comment of this sort. It's not going to assist the trial. If Mr. Milosevic chooses to ask you about it, then you can answer, but it doesn't assist at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These are all the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn now and sit again in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Matovina, is it true that in -- until 1990s you were one of the prominent members of the League of Communists in your area?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I was a member of the League of Communists or, rather, the Social Democratic Party just as the majority of those who were on the police force at the time. It was then called the militia, of course. I was not a leading member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you were a member of the League of Communists. For how long?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fifteen years. In your statement, you said that you were acting chief of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Slatina in 1989 and 1990.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: From 1988 to 1990 when the former chief was appointed president of the municipality, and the same Communist Party did not give me approval on moral grounds to become chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you were replaced by the HDZ, not the Communist Party.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They did not replace me because I had never been appointed. I was acting chief very briefly before the new chief that we discussed was appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. This new chief who took your place, was that Stjepan Gujmerac?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. He took the job in 1990, and his predecessor was Kresimir Libl.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Stjepan Gujmerac, who was a member of the HDZ, took your job?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know if he was a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were chief, you were engaged in public security jobs.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many Serbs were there in 1989 and 1990 in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I have already said something about the ethnic composition in the former municipality of Slatina. It was 57 per cent of Croats, 36 per cent of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm talking about the town itself.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, in the town of Slatina, I believe the ratio was a bit different, something like 48 per cent of Croats and 40 -- I can't really remember how many Serbs there were in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were in the majority in town, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the security situation while you were chief?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I have discussed that too. I said that with the first democratic elections, the security situation became more complex with every day, mainly in terms of propaganda and psychological activities that emanated primarily from the leadership of the SDS and some of the insurgent Serbs who refused to accept the results of the election and the introduction of the democracy because, under communist rule, they used to have the upper hand in politics, defence, economy, and occupied all the leading positions, although they were in the minority in the area of Slatina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it became more and more complex. Do you mean to say that after the elections, the situation deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that after the HDZ came into power, you became one of the vehicles of violence against the Serbs; illegal arrests, violence, seizure of property, expulsions, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: That is not true. Back then, and today as well, I had many friends among the Serbs, and they could always find in me a good collaborator on the job, a good colleague, and a friend. If you are talking about tolerance and broad-mindedness, I believe I have these qualities, and I believe hundreds of Serbs from where I come from can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, is it true that you played a prominent role in the arrests of over 400 Serbs and their detention in the investigative prison in Osijek? Those were mostly prominent intellectuals and renowned people who were arrested for the only reason that they were Serbs. Do you know that there are witnesses who can testify to that, that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Remain on the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- tied them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question you were asked was, first of all, this: It says you played a prominent role in the arrest of over 400 Serbs and their detention in prison in Osijek. Can you help us with that as to whether that's right or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not true. Over the past few years, when work was done on investigation of the armed insurgency, I didn't do all the work. A lot of material was gathered in the investigative centre. Sixty to 70 persons were detained, and after being processed, they were either released or exchanged. I don't know exactly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what happened to them, but they were turned over to the judiciary, and I didn't handle these investigations myself. I didn't touch the hair of one single Serb's head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "taken into custody," that means arrested, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I mean persons who participated in armed insurgency and about whom we had evidence that they had been members of the units that we have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you whether "taken into custody" means arrested.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They were brought before the investigative judge in order to give a statement, following regular procedure. There are documents about that compiled by the police, again following procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that among those people who were detained, there was Milan Jorgic, who is now director of the elementary school in Backi Brijeg, Tine Jorgic, and Mica Bozo Jovic and others? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with these names, although as far as this Jorgic is concerned, I know him, but I don't know that he had ever been arrested or taken into custody. But if it had been done, it was done according to procedure, legal procedure, and this must be on record in the Prosecutor's office. There is appropriate evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Ivan Fekete also took part in this violence against the Serbs? This man frequently beat Serbs who were tied up in a lavatory that was turned into a prison.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: That's not true. Ivan Fekete is a police inspector who simply doesn't behave in that way. I know that man personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that Milan Jorgic used to work in the elementary school in Slatina but due to being beaten up and attacks by your group, he had to leave Croatia although he wished to stay?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I'm not aware that Milan Jorgic was ever beaten up or that any pressure at all was brought to bear upon him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Is it true, according to statements of refugees from Slatina, that you were one of the organisers of the ethnic cleansing against Serbs in that area?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Of course not. If I had any say in it, there would never have been a war in the first place. My world views are entirely different from what you are trying to suggest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You are claiming that Serbs in the area of Podravska Slatina did not have much education. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No, it is not. I was only saying that the extremist wing of the SDS skilfully indoctrinated and used some Serbs - not all of them - for their own purposes and made their actions so radical that it had an impact on the further course of armed insurgency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that they manipulated these people who were mostly poorly educated?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They did manipulate a certain number of people. I never generalised anything, and I never spoke about collective responsibility or anything else in collective terms in relation to any nation at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that it was precisely in Slatina, speaking of intellectuals, there were many more intellectuals among Serbs than among Croats?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, I never counted intellectuals in either group, but it is a fact that all managers in larger enterprises were Serbs. For 45 years after the previous war, the chief of the police station in Slatina could not be a Croat. Heads of departments in the national defence secretariat were always Serbs. All the key positions in the town and in the territory of the former municipality of Slatina were occupied by Serbs. Furthermore, Croats could not be officers except for very few in the JNA. You get my drift, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that after the new government came into power, the key positions continued to be occupied by Serbs, including the police, the army, public services?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. And there is evidence of that. In all key positions and in the majority of state organs in the economy and government, you only had Serbs. For instance, in Krapina, for 30 to 40 years a Serb was the chief of police. Customs officers and the head of the customs office, all of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about other places except Krapina? Do you know how many Slovenes held such positions on boarder crossings?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I didn't count. It is a matter of common knowledge. These issues were widely written about in the press in Croatia, in Bosnia, in Slovenia. That was common knowledge all those years. And as the years went by, the issue came to the fore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the press," you mean propaganda.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, not all of the press is propaganda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us not engage in a general debate. Tell me, do you know a prominent citizen of Slatina, a Serb, a lawyer by profession, Milan Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know the man personally. I believe he's from Orahovica, but I never had any personal contact with him. I don't know where he is nowadays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But is it true -- you were in the police, after all, at the time; is it true that before the war he was president of the Municipal Court in Orahovica and, after that, president of the District Court in Slavonska Pozega?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know the positions he occupied because he came from the area of Orahovica and I never had any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in 1991, after the HDZ came into power, he was replaced from the position of president of the District Court in Slavonska Pozega and opened his own law office returning to Slatina where you were chief of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I told you what position I occupied before the war and for how long. But that doesn't matter now. I have already answered that I had no contact with Milan Vukovic, and I don't even know that he is in Slatina today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that in August 1991, by a group from the ZNG and a group of citizens from Rostas, he was arrested and taken to your police station?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that. I never heard about the event, nor did I ever see him on the premises of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that it was precisely you who attended his torture in the SUP when he was threatened with a knife, left to lie on the bare concrete floor and cigarette butts were thrown onto his body? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No, and I can swear to that. It never happened. I never witnessed anything like that, nor did I do anything like that, nor could I have done anything like that, and I am prepared to swear to it on my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to my information, it was precisely in your police station that he as a peace-loving citizen, a lawyer, former president of a court, a model citizen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said it is not true. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know that he was systematically beaten and that he could not walk for months? From his toes up to the top of his head, he was beaten up all over.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know about that. And I certainly do not know anything about this. In my life, I did not even torture an animal, let alone a human being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that Ante Simara was president of the municipal committee of the HDZ in the period that you referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. He was in charge of the government and he was president of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you held the position that you did, I assume that you have to know that this man was the main protagonist of systematic intimidations and an entire series of crimes against the Serbs in the area of Slatina. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. I know that he was an MP, that he was the deputy of the government when six members of the Executive Council who were Serbs walked out of the Executive Council and in this way blocked the work of the Assembly and the Executive Council. At that time, the government had to appoint a special deputy to be in charge and he was the one. I don't know about what you've been referring to, these intimidations, tortures, and I can't remember what else you said. I don't know about that. I cannot confirm that. That certainly is not true, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what happened to a local Serb, Nikola Kosic, who was then employed at the Jugobanka branch office in Slatina? You'd have to know in all probability that this man was killed in the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes. And this crime was investigated. Persons were brought in for questioning and were even convicted subsequently. Court proceedings were initiated and carried out. That is to say, both the police and the court acted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the perpetrators of his murder were actually sentenced?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They were, and there are also valid legal judgements to prove that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give me the names of the perpetrators who were actually convicted and sentenced.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. There are several persons who were tried, and later on, when there was abolition or, rather, when a large number of citizens who were ethnic Serbs were abolitioned for the crimes they had committed, then a number of members of the Croatian army were also included in this abolition by the Croat authorities. But for a while they were in prison, and they had been convicted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your reference to "abolition," is that to amnesty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the murderers of Mr. Kostic you say were convicted but in due course they were amnestied. Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After having been in prison for a while, their sentences were reduced or, rather, they did not serve their entire sentences, the ones from the judgement that had been passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you were in the top echelons of the police, I assume that you would have to know about the killing of Milutin Gunjevic, which was committed in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were his murderers ever brought to justice?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: In that period, as I already said, it is true that several murders were committed. The Croatian authorities condemned this rigorously, and this was done during this general turmoil when the town was full of refugees, when massacres took place, killings, shellings, and when during this general commotion during the war the police could not prevent all these cases. However, as far as all these cases are concerned, there are relevant files, on-site investigations were carried out, and all these files were submitted to the public prosecutor's office. So some investigations are under way until the present day, and some perpetrators were brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But the killers of Milutin Gunjevic were never brought before a court of law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They were not found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, they were not found?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They were not identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me who killed -- or, rather, was the killer of Gojko Oljaca ever captured?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We cannot go through every single event, serious as though they may be, and murder cases. We are dealing with a much broader spectrum here of events. What the witness has said is that there were murders, he accepted that, during the turmoil, as he put it, and the police couldn't prevent all the cases. Now, we cannot deal with every single incident in Slatina during this time. If you want to put it, put it in a general way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, what I mean is that if we're talking about a very small place like Slatina, if this witness was chief of police, he would really have to know about an entire series of murders of prominent Serbs from his town. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. How many Serbs are you suggesting, prominent Serbs in Slatina, were murdered? Just give us the overall figure and we'll put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, how many Serbs were killed, then, in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. There were killings of both Serbs and Croats. All of this happened, as I already described, during this general turmoil that prevailed during war. And I said that had the police not acted to the extent it had acted, it is certain that there would have been even more murders, primarily because all these people who came to the area without a thing in their hands came with all their frustrations as well. They were outsiders. They were refugees from Vukovar and Ilok. They were ex-police from Kosovo and Vojvodina, not to mention the fury that was escalating day after day because of all the massacres and killings that were taking place in the occupied area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please; you claim that somebody was expelled from Serbia. Do you know that that is not correct and that no one was expelled from Serbia? From Kosovo to Vojvodina, nobody was expelled from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know, then, why all these refugees came from Kosovo, why they all came to Croatia. Also, I don't know why Croats from Vojvodina, from Hrtkovci and from the other villages there, those people who came with tears in their eyes and little shopping bags in their hands, why did they come to look for houses in Slavonia so that they could exchange their own? Why did they talk about pressures that were exerted against them in Serbia? Grenades were thrown into their yards, they were threatened with murder, and there were other forms of exerting force that can actually be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of a single case of a murder? Are you aware of any murder of any Croat in Serbia? Were any of their houses torched or were they beaten up or any such thing?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: There were thousands of refugees, hundreds of them that were coming in. I did not carry out all the investigations on my own. I did not summarise all this information by myself, but all the information is there, and it is certain that they did not come of their own free will. And how did this happen to occur during the war and during the armed rebellion that Croats came from Vojvodina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all a matter of argument, Mr. Matovina, and in due course, we're going to have to decide. As far as you're concerned, you can go no further than saying that these refugees arrived in Slatina, and no doubt this is what they told you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have an explanation as to why the well-known anti-fascist Stanko Garaca was killed in Slatina, a holder of the 1941 Partizan Memorial Medal. I'm sure that you knew him.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I assumed that he was killed by perpetrators unknown during those first days of the conflict. We carried out an extensive investigation, however, the perpetrators were never found. This case is still being dealt with by the public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, Mr. Matovina, all these killings of Serbs who were residents of Slatina is something that you do know about, being chief of police there. Do you claim that you could not have done a thing in order to establish who the perpetrators of the killings were and to bring them to justice?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: As for certain murders, we did find the perpetrators, and also for certain incidents that were a safety and security problem, namely the burning of houses, damaging houses, et cetera. We certainly didn't resolve all the cases, but for those that we did know about, we did not conceal anything, and we did take measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But without any results; is that right, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: You are talking about murders that took place during the war. Do you think -- I mean, I think that as the architect of this war, you would have had to know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Matovina, we can't really go into this argument. Just deal with the matters that you can give evidence about, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, are you trying to say that Slatina was a theatre of war and that in this war that was waged in Slatina, there were killings of these Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: It is certain that Slatina was a theatre of war because systematically from the occupied area, it was shelled. I said already that there were over 400 artillery attacks, also aircraft attacks. Also there were infiltrations of persons from the occupied area. Then also there was a case when a railway was blown up, a railroad, when a train was supposed to pass through there during the night. All these killings and massacres that I have referred to, I think that at that time a person had to be in Slatina in any position in order to realise what war really meant and what wars brought along with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know precisely in Slatina that these Ustasha group of Tugomir Benes and Sinisa Kosutic carried out many torchings and expulsions of Serb houses precisely in the territory of your municipality where you headed the police. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: It is certain that various localities were blown up and we tried to prevent this from happening. And if it did happen, we brought the perpetrators to justice. Also with this small number of policemen that we had, we made a maximum preventive effort in order to reduce the number of such cases to the greatest possible degree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many such cases that you referred to, and there were few of them according to your records, how many of them were there actually, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I told you that I did not carry out all the investigations by myself. And as you say -- I mean, I told you that I held a particular position, but I did carry it out with full responsibility and with all my other co-workers to the extent possible during a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you do not know how many houses were blown up, torched in the area where you were chief of police and so on and so forth, in addition to the murders that you did not manage to resolve?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact number, but there are precise figures at the police station. That is to say that these cases were dealt with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Give us an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I cannot, because I would be misquoting the figure involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it three houses or 300 houses or 3.000 houses?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: It's not three, it's not 300, it's not 3.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So approximately we're talking about which order of magnitude?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I said I cannot tell you the number. I would be giving you wrong information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you deny the fact that entire Serb villages, for example, Gornji Miholjac, Somborje, Greda, Medinci, Aleksandrovac [phoen] were totally destroyed, levelled to the ground?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When? When, Mr. Milosevic, are you putting that this happened so that we may understand your case? Did this happen before or after the war, as it's been called? Before or after December 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is precisely in the time that this witness is talking about, Mr. May. That is to say, the year is 1991. That's the year that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let the witness deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not correct. These villages still exist. People live there and one can go and take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not correct that these villages were levelled to the ground? These are Serb villages. Who lives there now?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They're not levelled to the ground. People live there. The same people who lived there, or those who exchanged houses or bought houses depending on the circumstances involved how people resolved questions pertaining to their status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Serbs are there in these villages now, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. You're asking me too much. I did not keep such records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know who is behind these crimes of destroying these Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The perpetrators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Just a moment. You cannot misrepresent the evidence, Mr. Milosevic, something you're guilty of frequently. The witness just said the villages weren't destroyed, so you can't then put a question saying that they were. But one of the things which the accused put earlier, Mr. Matovina, was this, that there was what he called a Ustasha band who was responsible for crimes. Against Serbs, that is. Was there such a band or something like it? Were there people going around committing these crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not correct. Sinisa Kosutic, that Mr. Milosevic mentioned, was in the military police. He's an ethnic Serb. How could he go around blowing up Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about this other group of Tugomir Benes?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Tugomir Benes was also on the reserve police force. He was never involved in such things, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So neither Kosutic nor Benes. And you claim on the basis of what Mr. May just said due to the best of his understanding, that the villages I mentioned to you were not destroyed. That's how he understood you.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The villages were not destroyed. Some houses were blown up in some of these villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And am I mistaken if I say that in none of these villages was there ever a single member of the TO or was a single bullet fired or were there any war operations, these villages that I referred to? Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Some members of the TO were precisely from these villages, and after these massacres were carried out, there was the possibility of revenge, of retaliation by certain persons, and everybody was fully aware of it. So we acted in a preventive fashion so that such things would not happen in these villages, or at least to the least extent possible. That is the instructions on which the police operated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you did not answer my question. But is it true that there were no war operations in these villages or that there were no armed formations of any kind in these villages? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: That's right. There were no operations in these villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there was this destruction, and you say that it was only partial, not complete throughout these villages. Was this out of revenge, or how do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, probably it was out of revenge. I spoke about all the atrocities that took place, and it is quite possible and true that there were individual radicals and that it was difficult to leash them in, radicals against whom the police and the authorities were energetic in combatting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: Do you know about the fate of the villages Djurji [phoen], Sekulinci, Kometnik, Lisicine, Drenovac, Pusina, Krasovic? These are all Serb villages. Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: These villages, just like all the other ones, when the paramilitary units withdrew, the villages were damaged. As I've already said, the village of Cetekovac, Vocin, Hum, et cetera, Zvecevo and all the other villages in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were the perpetrators who did this?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Who did it? Well, this was done by the paramilitary units, the ones which were withdrawing. And quite certainly there were individuals as well on the Croatian side against whom we were struggling against and trying to prevent them from doing things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you claim that it was the Serbian paramilitaries who destroyed all the Serbian villages that I just enumerated, that I just read out?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, in part, yes. Who destroyed Vocin, for example, Hum, Cetekovac, Zvecevo, those villages?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm asking you. Who did do that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, I've given you an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was the Serbian paramilitary units which destroyed the Serbian villages; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, they destroyed everything in their path. They set fire to everything and killed the people who didn't want to join them and leave Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I heard you say a moment ago -- you mention the name of a Serb a moment ago who had allegedly been killed because he refused to go with them. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, in view of the fact that this is a very specific question: How many attacks on the JNA barracks were launched? The JNA barracks were right beside your police station, weren't they, in Slatina? So you can tell us that.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: There was not a single attack, and for our part, we had very good relations with them and didn't expect an attack at all. We didn't expect the attack that was to come to pass on the 4th of August, 1991. We considered that there were no grounds for that, no reason for an attack of that kind, because we thought that the army was going about its business and that there was no danger coming from the barracks, from that quarter. However, as I have already said, the intention was that when the transference of duty took place, that both the police shifts were to be destroyed, both those people going to take up their duties and take over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Matovina. From what you have said with respect to these actions, it would seem that only one policeman was injured in all that melee. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, are you talking about destruction and two shifts of the police force if only one policeman was wounded?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I've already said that on that particular occasion, the shift took place half an hour before the usual time of 2300 hours, and the gunfire from the heavy weapons and the armoured vehicles were directed to the premises where this takeover of duty was taking place, and this -- there were no policemen there, but this particular police officer, the one who was injured, was providing security for the building. The other policemen had left to perform their duty elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, from what you've just said, it would appear that they weren't informed. Were they inside? Were they not inside? How could they not have been informed if you yourself say that they were 50 metres away from the police station? And now say that the policemen had left the police station to carry out their duties on the ground. Do you really imagine that they weren't able to see from a distance of 50 metres that the policemen had left the station?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, the building was in darkness, and during the attack, they probably were not aware of the facts. As the attack was conducted precisely at that time when this shift taking over was to be conducted, the intention was clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what you're saying is that from a distance of 50 metres, they weren't able to see that the policemen had in fact left. Tell me this now: How long were the soldiers kept in the barracks under siege without food or water?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The soldiers had food and water the whole time they were kept there. The siege of the barracks followed on from the attack. It came after the attack launched at the police station or, rather, after the massacre had been committed in Cetekovac, because that particular massacre, the one we talked about a moment ago, was perpetrated on the 4th of September and the barracks were taken over on the 16th of September. So this was one week prior to the takeover of the barracks when the blockade was effected, because it was clear what the intentions were of the army. It was quite clear that in the barracks, preparations of the reservists had been conducted and that the weapons of the Territorial Defence which was in the warehouses within the compound --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're going a long way from the point, Mr. Matovina. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, you say that the siege went on for a week, until you took over the barracks. Just one week; right? So you kept the soldiers there without any electricity or water in those barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The soldiers did have electric power, water. Food was brought in to them at regular intervals. They had everything they required except for the fact that the telephone communications had been cut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Matovina, didn't you say during your examination-in-chief a moment ago that there was no JNA near that place called Cetekovci and everything that happened there, that you did not have any information with respect to a clash with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I told the truth, and I am telling the truth. I said what the role of the JNA was in the training of the reservists and the distribution of weapons, and I also talked about the attack on the police station and how this course of events took place and how it -- the barracks came to be taken over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you yourself say that there was no fighting, that the soldiers left the barracks when you took it over? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers went to their own houses, the rank and file, whereas the officers were allowed to leave. They were taken to Bjelovar, in fact, and they gave back what they were issued. And I said that one of the officers came in his own car. He was able to move around freely, and he came to pick up the pistol that he had left in the barracks. So nothing happened to any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no clash with the army, and the army left; right? And the fact that they opened fire on that particular day, that was to caution you, in fact, to warn you not to keep them in a blockade and that they didn't kill anybody. Is that so or not, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. That was on the 4th of August, and the blockade followed after the 4th of September, that is to say after the massacre in Cetekovac had taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the army had nothing to do with that. You said that too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: What I said was that it took part in the training of the reservists, that it distributed weapons, transported the convoy, and took the weapons around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally, Mr. Matovina, know nothing except the fact that all the recruits were trained from all parts of Yugoslavia, all those who were doing their military service; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, recruits are trained. However, it was unusual that it was precisely from the Slatina area and the area around Slatina that the reservists were called up, reservists of the Territorial Defence who were exclusively Serbs. They were called up for training in the barracks. That was unusual. And after the training had been completed, they took weapons off with them and went to the insurgent areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you come to know that?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, why wouldn't I? There was testimony from those officers or, rather, members of the TO who later returned and lived quite freely. They returned to their own houses and lived in their homes. I spoke about the law on amnesty as well, I mentioned that. And the return of the people who had previously left the region. So of course, all that later on became evident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's cut this short. Is it true that the attacks launched on the Serbs, against the Serbs and members of the army were conducted in general by paramilitary units of Ivica Belami and the other man Dzuro Decak? You must have known that as the chief of police, chief of SUP.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No, they are not from Slatina and they have nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're talking about things that don't concern Slatina alone. I'm not only asking you about that case in point, the one that took place in Slatina, but I'm asking you whether these units, the Belami and Decak units, whether you knew what they were engaged in, involved in.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, I said that I spent the entire war in Slatina. I said that a moment ago. And I also said loud and clear what jobs I performed during that time. So the Croatian army, at that time, was being established, and units, each in its own region, were responsible for the state of affairs, no doubt, and the assignments they were issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. So you know nothing about the activities of these paramilitary formations of Belami and Decak; is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: What do you mean "paramilitary"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, call them whatever you like. What I'm asking is do you know anything about the activities of those units? You say you know nothing. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to. I don't know of any specific case in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you in quite concrete terms what you know about the activities of the Belami and Decak units.

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: All I know is that in Virovitica, the problem there was the occupation of the barracks. The barracks were taken over by the National Guards Corps. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was this perpetrated by the two of them?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Not only the two of them but others as well. Other officers too. The Home Guard Corps, the ZNG, when the armed conflict broke out in Croatia with the JNA and when the JNA was threatened, then these units quite certainly blocked the JNA barracks and prevented them from going into action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. But you know when the order was given to block all the JNA barracks, that the JNA did not attack anybody and that it was in its own barracks on the Croatian section of its territory. Isn't that right, Mr. Matovina?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. All I do know is that the JNA took the side of part of the insurgent Serbs. It armed them. It bombed and shelled towns from the sea and from the air. And another thing I know is that, during that time, the entire Croatian people were proclaimed as the aggressor people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many Croats were members of the JNA at the time and how many Croatian generals were in the JNA and other high-ranking officers from Croatia? How many of them were members of the JNA, the JNA being composed of all the ethnic groups living in Yugoslavia, all the nations and nationalities?

utterances.speaker: DZURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many Croats there were. All I do know is that the ethnic composition was not proportionate to the population in the area of the former Yugoslavia, and I know who played the dominant role therein.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you mention that according to the memorandum issued by the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, there was some fabricated border of a Greater Serbia, that this is something that cropped up and stretched along the Karlobag-Karlovac-Virovitica line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's not given evidence about this. We've heard a great deal about this line from other witnesses, so I don't think we're going to be assisted by asking something he has not given evidence about. He hasn't mentioned it in his evidence.
